## Guided Tutorial 2.2: Examining the Charles River Accounting Core for Completeness and Consistency

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will examine the Charles River Accounting Core tables to assess whether the general ledger entries and chart of accounts are complete and consistent. This is a more accounting-specific data quality assessment than the O2C tutorial, because it involves checking whether the accounting records themselves are internally coherent. The skills practiced here connect directly to the audit analytics you will perform in the Excel chapters of Part II and the SQL chapters of Part III.

**Prerequisites.** You need Microsoft Excel installed on your computer, access to the CharlesRiver.xlsx file, and completion of Tutorial 2.1.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1.** Open CharlesRiver.xlsx in Excel (if not already open) and click on the Account worksheet. Examine the columns available. You should see fields including AccountID, AccountNumber, AccountName, AccountType, AccountSubType, and ParentAccountID. This is the chart of accounts for Charles River, and it forms the backbone of the Accounting Core. The ParentAccountID column creates a hierarchical structure that organizes accounts into groups. Scroll through the list to get a sense of how many accounts exist and how they are organized.

**Step 2.** Check the chart of accounts for completeness. Every major account type should be represented. Sort or filter the AccountType column and verify that the chart includes accounts classified as Asset, Liability, Equity, Revenue, and Expense. If any major category is missing, that is a completeness problem. Record your findings.

**Step 3.** Click on the GLEntry worksheet. Examine the columns available. You should see fields including GLEntryID, PostingDate, AccountID, Debit, Credit, VoucherType, VoucherNumber, SourceDocumentType, SourceDocumentID, SourceLineID, CostCenterID, FiscalYear, and FiscalPeriod. Scroll down to get a sense of the volume of data. The GLEntry worksheet holds hundreds of thousands of rows, close to the maximum that a single Excel worksheet can contain.

**Step 4.** Check the general ledger for a fundamental accounting consistency requirement: for every transaction, total debits should equal total credits. To test this at the aggregate level, use the SUM function to calculate the total of the Debit column and the total of the Credit column. The two totals should be equal, or very nearly so (small differences may arise from rounding). If there is a significant difference, that indicates a serious consistency problem in the ledger.

**Step 5.** Check for accounts referenced in the general ledger that do not exist in the chart of accounts. This is a referential integrity test (@tbl-02-03). With hundreds of thousands of rows, adding a formula to every GLEntry row would be slow, so work with distinct values instead. Insert a PivotTable from the GLEntry worksheet and place AccountID in the Rows area. The PivotTable lists each AccountID that appears in the ledger exactly once. Next to the PivotTable, use XLOOKUP or COUNTIFS to check whether each listed AccountID exists in the Account worksheet's AccountID column. Any AccountID with no match is an orphaned reference. In the Charles River data, every AccountID should match. A clean result like this is still a finding worth recording, because it tells you that the ledger's account references can be relied on.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A single Excel worksheet can hold just over one million rows, and the Charles River GLEntry table already fills most of that space. Formulas copied down every row of a table this size can make Excel slow or unresponsive. Summarizing first, as the PivotTable in Step 5 does, keeps the workbook responsive. When a dataset outgrows Excel altogether, SQL becomes the better tool, which is one reason Part III teaches it.
:::

**Step 6.** Examine the PostingDate column. Sort by posting date and note the earliest and latest dates. Then build a PivotTable with FiscalYear and FiscalPeriod in the Rows area and a count of GLEntryID in the Values area. Most periods contain a similar volume of entries, but the first period and the final periods contain far fewer. Before treating a low-volume period as a sign of missing transactions, check whether it sits at the edge of the extract. The data begins when the company's records begin and ends early in a new fiscal year, so those periods are partial by construction. Filter to the latest fiscal year and look at the SourceDocumentType of its entries. Record what you find and whether these entries belong in an analysis of the fiscal years under review, which is a timeliness and cutoff question.

**Step 7.** Examine the Debit and Credit columns for missing or unusual values. Filter for rows where both the Debit and Credit fields are zero. You will find a small number of such rows, all from the same source document type. An entry with no debit and no credit amount serves no accounting purpose. It may be a system artifact or a data entry error, and either way it should be investigated and explained. Record the count and the source document type.

**Step 8.** Examine the SourceDocumentType column. Use a PivotTable to count the number of GLEntry rows for each source document type. You should see types such as "SalesInvoice," "Shipment," "PurchaseInvoice," "GoodsReceipt," "MaterialIssue," "PayrollPayment," "JournalEntry," and "WorkOrderClose." If an expected source type were absent, that would indicate a completeness problem, in which an entire business cycle failed to post to the ledger. Record the distribution of entries by source document type.

**Checkpoint.** At this point, you should have assessed the Charles River Accounting Core against the quality dimensions in @tbl-02-03. For completeness, you checked that all account types are present in the chart of accounts, that every period has entries (and why some periods are small), and that every expected source document type appears in GLEntry. For consistency, you confirmed that debits equal credits in the aggregate and that every GL account reference exists in the chart of accounts. For accuracy and timeliness, you identified the zero-amount rows and the entries dated beyond the fiscal years under review. Your findings should be documented in a brief written summary that identifies each test performed, the result, and any issues discovered, including the tests that found no problems. This exercise previews the audit analytics work in Parts II and III, where you will use Excel and then SQL to automate these same tests across the entire population.
